story.headline: The dollar rose for a fifth straight day to its highest since April 2025 as Fed officials kept warning on inflation. Weak growth figures from Japan and China barely moved markets.

reads.policy: Another Fed official, Kansas City's Jeff Schmid, warned that inflation is moving the wrong way, and a December Fed hike now looks all but certain. In Japan, board member Hajime Takata called for an early hike despite a shrinking economy. Europe, Britain and Japan are also expected to hike, but US rates are rising faster, which keeps favouring the dollar.
reads.growth: Japan's economy shrank slightly in the summer and China's October spending and factory figures all fell short. Neither moved currencies much, but weaker Chinese demand is a quiet drag on the Aussie and kiwi. The US economy still looks firmer, and US retail sales on Tuesday are the next check.
reads.inflation: US inflation is still running far above the Fed's goal, which keeps the pressure to hike and supports the dollar. Canada's October inflation this morning decides whether a December Bank of Canada hike comes back into view. UK inflation on Wednesday matters just as much for the pound.
reads.risk: Iran's weekend claims of a sunk supertanker and strikes in Bahrain went unconfirmed, and US stock futures rose at the open. With markets calm, the safe-haven franc and yen got no lift. The Aussie and kiwi, which track market mood and China, stayed near their lows.
reads.tot: Oil slipped as traders trusted the forecast of a supply surplus more than unconfirmed war claims. Cheaper oil eases the strain on energy buyers like Japan and the euro area and takes a little support from the Canadian dollar. Gold faded back below $3,900, offering the Aussie little help.
reads.positioning: Hedge funds lean toward the dollar and against the kiwi, the Canadian dollar and the euro, and the dollar's run keeps paying them. Their large bet on the yen keeps losing money as it weakens. A delayed weekly report from US regulators is due this afternoon.
reads.fiscal: Record US government borrowing keeps long-term US borrowing costs above 5%. Higher yields support the dollar for now, but a growing deficit is a worry if buyers start asking for more. France's debt troubles keep weighing on the euro.

fed.summary: The Federal Reserve held rates on October 28 with two officials voting to hike. Hot inflation and a run of firm talk from officials have made a December hike all but certain and lifted the dollar to its highest since April 2025.
fed.priced: December: hike all but certain, a half-point move a small minority bet; more hikes expected next year.
fed.why: US inflation is running at about twice the Fed's 2% goal, and Kansas City Fed President Jeff Schmid says it is moving the wrong way. Officials keep lining up behind more hikes.
fed.watch: Fed Chair Kevin Warsh speaks today at 11:00 AM CT, then US retail sales Tuesday and the October meeting minutes Wednesday. The decision is December 9.

boc.summary: The Bank of Canada raised rates to 2.50% in October and said more may be needed. Two months of job losses have made a December hike doubtful, so today's inflation figures matter.
boc.priced: December: hold is the base case; hike about one in three.
boc.why: Inflation is expected to stay above 3% through much of next year, but Canada's economy has stalled and is shedding jobs.
boc.watch: Canadian inflation for October, out today at 7:30 AM CT; a hot reading would revive the December hike. The decision is December 9.

rbnz.summary: The Reserve Bank of New Zealand held at 2.75% in October in a narrow vote. Rising unemployment has made a December hike less certain, and the kiwi sits near a 19-month low.
rbnz.priced: December: hike possible but not fully expected.
rbnz.why: Inflation pressures argue for a hike, but unemployment at its highest since 2015 argues for waiting.
rbnz.watch: New Zealand inflation expectations tonight at 8:00 PM CT and Governor Anna Breman's speech Wednesday. The decision is December 9.

ecb.summary: The European Central Bank held at 2.50% in October and a December hike is widely expected. Economists see it as the last for now, which leaves the euro trailing as US rates keep rising.
ecb.priced: December: hike widely expected, possibly the last for a while.
ecb.why: Euro-area inflation is about double the bank's goal, but growth is only modest and France's debt worries linger, so the bank has little room to keep hiking.
ecb.watch: President Christine Lagarde speaks Wednesday, Thursday and Friday. The decision is December 17.

boj.summary: The Bank of Japan holds at 1.25%, far below other major banks, and is expected to hike in December. Board member Hajime Takata called for an early move even as Japan's economy shrank slightly in the summer.
boj.why: The weak yen is pushing import costs and prices up, and Takata says hikes are needed so it does not weaken further. A shrinking economy is the main reason to wait.
boj.watch: Whether Japan buys yen if the dollar tops 160 again, and Governor Kazuo Ueda's speech on November 30. The decision is December 18.

rba.summary: The Reserve Bank of Australia raised rates to 4.85% on November 3, the highest among the major banks, but hinted it may now pause. Weak Chinese figures and a rising dollar pushed the Aussie to its lowest since January.
rba.priced: December: no firm pricing yet; the bank itself hinted at a pause.
rba.why: Inflation is above the bank's forecasts, but unemployment is at a five-year high and demand from China, Australia's biggest customer, is softening.
rba.watch: Governor Michele Bullock speaks today at 4:50 PM CT; Australian jobs figures follow Wednesday at 6:30 PM CT. The decision is December 8.

boe.summary: The Bank of England raised Bank Rate to 4.00% on November 5 and said more may follow. Markets still expect a second hike in December, though the pound has slipped as US rates rise faster.
boe.priced: December: a second hike more likely than not.
boe.why: High energy costs from the Middle East conflict keep UK inflation up, and solid growth means the bank need not fear its hike is hurting the economy.
boe.watch: UK wage figures Tuesday at 1:00 AM CT and October inflation Wednesday at 1:00 AM CT, then Governor Andrew Bailey speaks twice. The decision is December 17.

snb.summary: The Swiss National Bank holds its rate at zero and can sell francs if they get too strong. Low Swiss inflation means no hike is in sight.
snb.why: Swiss inflation is barely above zero, so the bank has no reason to raise rates and some room to cut if the franc climbs.
snb.watch: Any flare-up that sends money into the franc. The decision is December 10.

USD.summary: The dollar sits in the middle of the board: rate and inflation support are partly offset by Democratic control of Congress. A fifth straight rise has taken it to its highest since April 2025 as Fed officials keep calling for hikes.

notes.policy: A December Fed hike is all but certain, and officials keep talking about more rises next year.
notes.inflation: US inflation is running at about twice the Fed's goal, which keeps pressure on it to raise rates.
notes.fiscal: With Democrats controlling Congress, President Trump's spending plans look harder to pass, which trims some support for the dollar.

EUR.summary: The euro sits near the bottom of the board: weak growth, dear energy and France's debt worries outweigh an expected December rate hike. Rising US rates have pushed it to its lowest since April 2025.

notes.policy: A December European Central Bank hike is expected and may be the last for a while, while US rates keep rising, so the gap works against the euro.
notes.growth: Euro-area growth held at a modest pace in the summer, but business surveys have weakened and France's economy is struggling.
notes.inflation: Euro-area inflation is about double the bank's goal, which keeps a December hike on the table.
notes.tot: The euro area buys most of its energy abroad, so dear oil drains money out of the region, though the recent fall in prices eases that.
notes.positioning: Speculators hold one of their biggest bets against the euro in years, so good news could set off a sharp rebound as they close it.
notes.fiscal: France's high debt and shaky budget keep investors demanding extra pay to hold French bonds, which weighs on the euro.

GBP.summary: The pound sits near the top of the board after the Bank of England raised rates to 4.00% and signalled more may follow. Faster-rising US rates have still held it near a three-week low ahead of UK inflation figures on Wednesday.

notes.policy: The Bank of England hiked in November, and its governor said it is unlikely to be the last while the Middle East conflict lasts.
notes.growth: UK growth matched forecasts in the third quarter and business surveys are the strongest since February, even though shoppers have pulled back.
notes.inflation: UK inflation is at its highest in about a year, keeping pressure on the Bank of England.

JPY.summary: The yen sits low on the board because Japanese rates are far below others and Japan pays dearly for imported energy. A likely December rate hike and warnings from Japan's finance minister help only a little with the dollar near 160 yen.

notes.policy: The Bank of Japan's rate is far below others, and even the December hike its board members are calling for leaves a wide gap with US rates.
notes.risk: The yen tends to gain when stock markets get scared, as they did in early November, and loses some of that pull when they calm.
notes.tot: Japan buys almost all its energy abroad, so oil holding near recent highs weighs on the yen.
notes.positioning: Speculators hold one of their biggest bets on the yen in years, and those bets lose money as the yen weakens, which could make them close fast.

CHF.summary: The franc sits in the middle of the board: its safe-haven pull is offset by inflation too low to need higher rates. The Swiss National Bank also says it can sell francs if they get too strong.

notes.inflation: Swiss inflation is low, so the central bank has no need to raise rates from zero.
notes.risk: The franc draws money when markets get nervous, but with stocks broadly holding up it has had little of that support lately.

AUD.summary: The Aussie scores well on the board thanks to the highest rates among the major central banks. It still fell to its lowest since January as US rates rose and China's economy showed fresh signs of slowing.

notes.policy: Australia's interest rate is the highest among the major central banks, though the governor hinted at a pause and some economists see the hikes ending.
notes.growth: Australian unemployment is at a five-year high, and weaker spending and factory output in China, its biggest customer, add to the drag.
notes.inflation: Inflation is running above the Reserve Bank of Australia's forecasts, which kept it hiking.
notes.tot: Australia sells energy and metals abroad, but gold's slide below $4,000 takes some of that support away.
notes.positioning: Speculators are betting heavily against the Aussie, so better news could set off a sharp rebound as they close those bets.

CAD.summary: The Canadian dollar sits mid-board: the Bank of Canada's October hike and oil exports help, but job losses have cut bets on more hikes. Canadian inflation figures out today decide whether a December hike comes back into view.

notes.policy: The Bank of Canada raised rates in October and says more may be needed, though its meeting notes added no new signal and markets doubt a December move.
notes.growth: Canada lost jobs in September and October, and growth has stalled.
notes.inflation: Rising costs for Canadian producers point to more inflation ahead.
notes.tot: Oil has held well above pre-war levels, which gives the loonie a cushion, though forecasts of a supply surplus are pulling prices down.

NZD.summary: The kiwi sits low on the board because rising unemployment has cut bets on a December rate hike. Rising US rates and weaker Chinese demand have kept it close to its lowest in 19 months.

notes.growth: New Zealand's unemployment rose to its highest since 2015.
notes.tot: Firm prices for dairy, New Zealand's main export, support its earnings, though China's spending is slowing.
notes.positioning: Speculators are betting heavily against the kiwi, so better news could set off a sharp rebound as they close those bets.
